newsitem.title: SPAIN: LME makes progress implementing SIB changes - CEO.
newsitem.headline: LME makes progress implementing SIB changes - CEO.

text.p: The London Metal Exchange (LME) has carried out around half of the changes asked for by Britain's Securities and Investments Board (SIB) in last December's review of the market, with more to come, chief executive David King said.
"We are halfway through the process (review), and we believe we have made progress," King said at Metal Bulletin's 10th International Copper Conference.
The LME has already changed the structure of its Board, instituted daily stock reporting, which seems to be working well, and just reecntly turned its attention to its sub- committees, King said.
The SIB review was asked for by the LME at the time of the Sumitomo Corp scandal and the firm's losses of $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper trading.
King said the affair had a marked impact on the LME, as did the tin crisis a decade earlier. Unlike the tin crisis, the LME has emerged in better shape.
"The LME will be a better, stronger, and more attractive global market," he said.
On Tuesday, continuing its reforms, the LME announced the names of additional people to serve on its various committees, which will now have more influence.
"They will have more authority to come to views and recommend them to the Board which will implement them," King said.
The warehousing committee, for instance, will be carrying out a review of the LME's entire delivery network as well as considering potential new locations in coming weeks.

This committee will also look at current warehousing practices, and whether concerns over in/out charges, the speed of movement in and out, and the issue of metal in store but not registered are justified.
This is a difficult issue to address, although if a warehouse company indulged in practices that could be seen as breaching LME rules or U.K. regulations, the exchange may be able to act, he said.

On transparancy, the LME is enhancing its vendor feed system to help pre-trade transparency. On this, the Exchange is still considering whether to make more information available on holders of large market positions and stocks. But the issue of confidentiality has to be tackled with care.
"We do not want to put information into the public domain that will drive business away from the exchange," King said.
Regarding market-monitoring, the LME continues to mull over the position of historic price carries, although these only amount for one percent of its business.
But the market is introducing a new internal compliance system, costing one million stg, which will be able to analyse all the various data. This will be built in coming months, he said.
Meanwhile, the vexed issue of what constitutes market manipulation remains difficult to address. There had only been one case of this proven in the UK and just a handful in the U.S.
"We would hope to come up with clearer guidelines...as well as looking at rules to extend our reach off-exchange (over-the- counter market)," King said.
